name: Birth order and height

lead: Several studies have found that, on average, later-born children are a little shorter than their older siblings. People interested in height bring it up as one of the background factors that shapes how tall someone ends up, alongside genetics, nutrition and puberty timing.

The best-known study used Swedish military records for about 650,000 men and compared brothers within the same family. It found later-born brothers were shorter than firstborns, and that birth weight and length did not explain the gap.

paras: It is not a practice or product, so there is nothing to apply. Height-minded readers use it to understand why siblings differ, and researchers use it to study how family size, spacing and living standards affect growth.

There are no risks in the topic itself. The effect is an average across large groups and small in size, and it has varied between countries and birth cohorts, so it does not predict an individual's height.

angle.text: Studies report that firstborns are on average a little taller than later-born siblings. It is a background factor that cannot be changed, which people cite when comparing siblings or discussing what shapes final height.

lead: Birth order and height refers to research showing that, across large populations, firstborn children tend to be slightly taller than their later-born siblings [1][2][3].

In looksmaxxing and height discussions the idea appears as one of the non-genetic factors behind how tall someone ends up. Height is something many people want to maximise, so factors that shift average adult height, even slightly, are of interest. Birth order is not something a person can change; its use is in explaining differences between siblings and expectations about growth.
The strongest evidence comes from a 2013 study of Swedish military conscripts. Work from India and other lower-income settings has examined related differences in childhood stunting [1][2][3].
infobox: Later-born shorter than firstborn on average [1][2]

paras: Birth order is a child's position in the sequence of births in a family. Researchers have studied whether it relates to personality, intelligence, health and physical traits. Broad reviews note that many claimed birth-order effects on personality have been challenged, while differences in some outcomes such as birth weight and adult socioeconomic position have been reported [4][1].

Researchers used the Swedish Military Conscription Register to analyse adult height of 652,518 men born from 1951 to 1983 [1][2]. Using fixed-effects models that compare brothers, they accounted for genetic and social factors shared within a family [1].

Their results showed later-born brothers were shorter than firstborn brothers. The gap was similar across family sizes and parental socioeconomic position, and smaller in more recent birth cohorts. Adjusting for birth weight and birth length did not explain it [2][1]. The authors suggested that improved living standards and shrinking family sizes may help explain population-level trends in height [2][1].

A 2021 paper in PNAS examining Indian children noted that second and later-born children often lag behind firstborns in height outcomes, especially in developing countries, and argued the difference is driven by short intervals between births [3]. Other studies of children in Lithuania, Japan and Brazil have included birth order among the factors examined for height and weight [5][6].

Height forums discuss birth order alongside genetics, nutrition, sleep and puberty timing as one of the circumstances that shape growth. Because it cannot be altered, it is mostly raised to explain differences between siblings.

The Swedish register study of 652,518 men found later-born brothers were shorter than firstborns, with birth weight and length not accounting for the difference [1][2]. A PNAS study of Indian children reported that birth-order differences in stunting were driven by short birth spacing [3]. These are observational studies; no trial can assign birth order.
